summary: Orbitly is a web game where you design, launch and fly a real-style space mission, alone or with a crew of up to four. You pick one of three missions powered by live NASA data: watching haze and wildfires around Malaysia (NASA EONET), warning Earth about solar storms (NASA DONKI), or flying past today's closest asteroid (NASA NeoWs). Then you build a spacecraft from real CubeSat-style parts, choose an orbit and a rocket, and fly it month by month while managing mass, power, budget, data, communications and lifetime. Every choice has a cost, and surprises like solar storms or a broken instrument test your design. At the end, a mission report scores you out of 100 and explains which earlier choice caused what, so you can redesign and fly again. Students rarely get to try a whole mission from idea to operation, so these trade-offs usually stay abstract. Orbitly lets them feel those trade-offs by trying, failing and improving.
details:
What it does

Orbitly is a space mission design game that runs in the browser on a laptop or phone. It follows the same four stages a real mission goes through: Design, Launch, Fly and Report. You can play solo, or host a team mission where up to four people build one spacecraft together, live.

How it works

1. Pick a mission (built on live NASA data). Each mission reads real NASA data while you play. Earth watch reads wildfires in Southeast Asia from NASA EONET and finds the one nearest to Kuala Lumpur, because haze is a real problem in Malaysia. Solar storm watch reads the latest coronal mass ejections from NASA DONKI. Asteroid scout uses NASA NeoWs to make today’s closest near-Earth asteroid your target. If NASA can’t be reached, the game falls back to a saved snapshot, so it always works. Players also choose a game mode (Cadet, Engineer, Director or Sandbox) and how many months to fly.

2. Design the spacecraft. You build the spacecraft step by step in 3D: frame (3U, 6U, 12U CubeSat or a microsatellite bus), solar panels, battery, flight computer, pointing system, radio, science instruments, orbit and rocket. Every part changes mass, power, cost and data. The part numbers sit inside the ranges in NASA’s State-of-the-Art of Small Spacecraft Technology report and the CubeSat Design Specification. Instruments made for a different mission only collect 20% of their science, so players have to match the payload to the goal. Before launch, a “Things to check” panel warns you, with a reason, if something won’t work.

3. Launch. You choose an orbit (low Earth, Sun-synchronous, geostationary, the Sun–Earth L1 point or deep space) and a rocket. Your chance of a good launch depends on the rocket’s reliability, whether it can lift your spacecraft, and whether Earth can hear your radio. Results range from a perfect launch to a countdown hold, a rocket failure or a lost signal.

4. Fly month by month. A dashboard tracks power, battery, storage, budget, health and science. Each month the panels make power, the battery covers Earth’s shadow, instruments collect data and the radio sends it home. You can pick a plan for each month (steady, push science or look after the spacecraft). Surprises such as fire and haze season, solar storms, space debris and instrument failures force you to make decisions, and some of these events come from the real NASA data. Science only counts once its data reaches Earth.

5. Mission report. The final score out of 100 is split into Mission success (40), Science value (25), Resource efficiency (20) and Handling surprises (15). Every part explains why you got that score, so players learn the reason behind the result, not just whether it was right or wrong. You can redesign and fly again, then post your score to the leaderboard.

6. Team mode. A host opens a room and up to four players join with a 6-digit code or a QR code. Each player takes a role: Mission Planner, Spacecraft Engineer, Science Lead, or Comms and Ops. Each role edits only its own part of the spacecraft, live. Big decisions go to a team vote, and a crew chat lets the team argue out competing priorities, just like a real mission team.

7. Learn inside the game. The Info section has a How to play guide, every item explained in 3D with “best when” and “watch out” notes, tips to win, and a Sources page listing every NASA dataset and report we used.

Benefits and intended impact

•        Makes mission design hands-on. Students learn systems engineering by doing it. They see that a bigger camera means more mass, power, data and cost, and that there is rarely one perfect build.

•        Teaches the why, not just right or wrong. Every warning and every score line explains the cause, so a failed mission still teaches something.

•        Locally relevant. The Earth watch mission is about the haze that affects Malaysia and Southeast Asia every year, so space science connects to something students actually live through.

•        Builds teamwork. Team mode gives each player real responsibility, so the crew has to negotiate, vote and coordinate like a real mission team.

•        Easy to reach. It runs in any browser, works on phones, needs no install, and the Cadet mode lets complete beginners start right away.

How it is creative

•        Live NASA data drives the missions and the surprise events, so every game reflects what is really happening on Earth, on the Sun and near Earth today.

•        The spacecraft is built piece by piece in 3D over a real Earth, and the launch is animated from the pad to orbit.

•        A real-time team mode with roles, votes and chat turns mission design into a group game.

•        Four game modes, from Cadet to Director plus a Sandbox, let the same game work for beginners and for players who want a challenge.

Factors we considered

•        Realism vs. simplicity: part numbers come from NASA ranges, rounded so they are easy to add up. Prices are game estimates, because NASA does not publish part prices.

•        Reliability: if a NASA API is down or slow, the game uses a saved snapshot of the data, so it never breaks during play.

•        Beginners: plain words, a step-by-step build, a “Things to check” list and tips, so players don’t need to know space engineering first.

•        Balance: we wrote tests that fly a winning build for each mission through the real game engine, so the game stays winnable when numbers change.

•        Mobile-friendly and easy to join: the layout is designed mobile-first, and teammates can join a team room by scanning a QR code or typing a 6-digit code.

Tools and technologies

React 19 and TypeScript with Vite, Tailwind CSS, Three.js with React Three Fiber and Drei for the 3D Earth, spacecraft, rockets and launch pad, Framer Motion for animation, and Zustand for game state. Supabase (Postgres database, anonymous sign-in, Realtime and database functions) powers team rooms, roles, voting, crew chat and the leaderboard. We used Vitest for tests and Vercel for hosting. All 3D spacecraft, rockets and the launch pad were drawn by our team in code.

Use of AI

We used Claude Code (an AI coding assistant) to help write, debug and review parts of the code, and to help draft and proofread text. The game idea, mission design, mechanics and scoring rules are our own, and the team reviewed and tested all AI-assisted work. No AI-generated images, video or audio are used.
